cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 2 · Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse

bullets.label: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: When nurses move into an international healthcare system, they are expected to apply safety standards consistently, explain the reasoning behind their actions, and respond appropriately when systems or practices place patients at risk.

bullets.label: This level bridges national nursing preparation
bullets.text: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations — strengthening your understanding of infection prevention, clinical risk, communication, documentation and culturally safe care.

bullets.label: Infection Prevention
Apply internationally recognised infection-prevention principles and aseptic technique during complex clinical care.
Risk & Escalation
Use risk assessment and clinical reasoning to prevent harm and recognise, escalate and document safety concerns.
Communication
Communicate safety information during handover and within multidisciplinary care environments.
Cultural Safety
Support patients and families to participate in safe care, adapting to diverse healthcare systems and policies.

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Beyond Task Completion

bullets.label: International practice requires nurses to
bullets.text: International practice requires nurses to recognise emerging risks, use evidence to guide care and communicate concerns assertively.

bullets.label: Safe International Practice Combines:
Competence — technical skills applied reliably across settings
Accountability — owning your decisions and their impact on the team
Adaptability — adjusting safely to new systems without compromising standards

cards.title: PROGRAMME OVERVIEW
cards.body: Your Learning Goal

bullets.label: By completing Level 2, you should be able to
bullets.text: By completing Level 2, you should be able to deliver safe, culturally responsive and evidence-informed nursing care while meeting the professional expectations of international healthcare environments.

bullets.label: International Standards
Risk Assessment
Communication
Culturally Safe Care

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Applying International Safety & Infection-Prevention Standards

bullets.label: Core Principle
While terminology and local procedures may
bullets.text: While terminology and local procedures may vary, the underlying principles remain consistent: prevent avoidable harm, use standard precautions, assess risk, communicate clearly and practise within professional standards.

bullets.label: Standards
Know local policy and professional guidelines
Consistency
Same safety behaviour across all shifts and settings
Evidence
Use current guidance, not outdated habits

cards.title: Safe Adaptation in a New Healthcare System
cards.body: Unfamiliar Technology

bullets.label: Ask for orientation to electronic records and medication systems before practising independently.
Use Supervision
Seeking supervised practice confirms competence within the organisation's approved process.
Seek Clarification
Asking for help demonstrates professionalism — not weakness. Confirm competence before independent practice.
Clinical Example: Latha, new to an overseas
bullets.text: Clinical Example: Latha, new to an overseas hospital, is asked to access an implanted port with unfamiliar equipment. She requests the local procedure and supervised practice first — protecting the patient while building her competence.

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Clinical Risk Assessment & Early Escalation

bullets.label: Dynamic Risk Assessment
Risk changes over time. A patient who was safe
bullets.text: Risk changes over time. A patient who was safe to mobilise in the morning may deteriorate by the afternoon. Assessment must be repeated when condition, treatment or environment changes.

bullets.label: Recognising Deterioration
Early warning signs include:
Altered respiratory rate or oxygen saturation
New confusion or reduced consciousness
Reduced urine output or fever
A general sense the patient is becoming unwell

cards.title: Escalation Using ISBAR
cards.body: I — Identify

bullets.label: State your name, role and the patient's name and ID.
S — Situation
Explain the current concern clearly and concisely.
B — Background
Give relevant history, diagnosis and recent changes.
A — Assessment
Share your clinical interpretation of the findings.
R — Recommendation
State what assistance or action you are requesting.
Escalation should continue if the response does
bullets.text: Escalation should continue if the response does not match the urgency of the concern. Patient and family observations are also valuable — their concerns should always be heard and assessed.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Safe Communication, Documentation & Incident Management

bullets.label: Communication failures contribute to many preventable incidents.
IQNs must provide accurate handover, document
bullets.text: IQNs must provide accurate handover, document care objectively, clarify uncertain instructions and report incidents through approved systems.

bullets.label: Handover — identify risks, recent changes, required monitoring and outstanding actions
Documentation — timely, factual and clearly attributable to the author
Closed-loop — receiver repeats the message; sender confirms accuracy

cards.title: Documentation & Incident Reporting
cards.body: What to Document

bullets.label: What was assessed, what action was taken, how
bullets.text: What was assessed, what action was taken, how the patient responded and who was informed. Use objective language — replace labels like "non-compliant" with factual descriptions.

bullets.label: Incident Reports
Complement — not replace — clinical
bullets.text: Complement — not replace — clinical documentation. Immediate patient care comes first. Reports record facts so patterns and contributing factors can be reviewed.

bullets.label: Near-Miss Reporting
Near misses reveal system weaknesses before
bullets.text: Near misses reveal system weaknesses before harm occurs. Reporting them is a professional responsibility and a key driver of quality improvement.

bullets.label: Clinical Example: A nurse receives an unclear
bullets.text: Clinical Example: A nurse receives an unclear telephone order for a high-risk medicine. She reads back patient details, medicine name, dose, route and timing. The prescriber corrects one digit — a near miss prevented through closed-loop communication.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Culturally Safe & Patient-Centred Care

bullets.label: Safety practices are most effective when
bullets.text: Safety practices are most effective when patients understand and can participate in them. Cultural beliefs, language, health literacy and prior healthcare experiences all influence communication and decision-making.

bullets.label: Communication Access
Use professional interpreters for complex or
bullets.text: Use professional interpreters for complex or high-risk conversations. Family members provide emotional support but may not translate accurately.

bullets.label: Shared Safety
Invite patients to confirm identity, report allergies, describe changes and ask whether hands have been cleaned.
Cultural Safety
Ask what matters to the patient rather than
bullets.text: Ask what matters to the patient rather than assuming beliefs. Accommodate preferences while explaining non-negotiable safety requirements.

cards.title: Teach-Back: Confirming Understanding
cards.body: What is Teach-Back?

bullets.label: Teach-back checks whether your explanation was
bullets.text: Teach-back checks whether your explanation was effective — it is not a test of the patient. Ask the patient to explain information in their own words or demonstrate a skill.

bullets.label: When to Use It
Medication instructions
Infection prevention at home
Wound and drain care at discharge
When to seek urgent help
Clinical Example: A patient with limited
bullets.text: Clinical Example: A patient with limited English is discharged with a wound drain. Using an interpreter and visual aids, the nurse asks the patient to demonstrate drain care. A misunderstanding is identified and corrected before discharge.

bullets.label: Safety Standards
Know your workplace policies, apply core safety behaviours consistently and use current evidence — not outdated habit.
Risk & Escalation
Assessment is continuous. Trends and subtle
bullets.text: Assessment is continuous. Trends and subtle changes matter. Use ISBAR to escalate clearly and listen to patients and families.

bullets.label: Communication
Clear handover supports continuity. Document
bullets.text: Clear handover supports continuity. Document facts and responses. Repeat back critical information and report near misses.

bullets.label: Cultural Safety
Provide communication support for high-risk
bullets.text: Provide communication support for high-risk information. Ask rather than assume. Use teach-back to confirm understanding.

cards.title: Ready for Level 3
cards.body: You have strengthened your ability to assess risk, apply international infection-prevention standards, communicate safety information and participate in incident management.

bullets.label: Level 3 moves from safe individual practice to leading safer systems and driving global quality improvement.
CONTINUE TO GNPS LEVEL 3

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 2: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments

bullets.label: Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse (IQN) · Student Learning Notes
SECTION 1
SAFETY & INFECTION PREVENTION

cards.title: Applying International Safety Standards
cards.body: International healthcare systems expect nurses to translate policies and evidence into reliable clinical behaviour. While terminology and local procedures may vary, the underlying principles remain universal: prevent avoidable harm, apply standard precautions, assess risk clearly, and practise within professional standards.

cards.title: Section Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Relate Local to Global
Link local workplace policies to broader international safety principles.
Apply Precautions
Consistently apply standard and transmission-based precautions in any setting.
Evidence-Based Practice
Recognise how guidelines and current evidence underpin safe clinical practice.
Safe Adaptation
Adapt safely and professionally when entering an unfamiliar healthcare system.

cards.title: CORE CONCEPT 1
cards.body: Standards & Local Policy

bullets.label: Every workplace operates within a framework of
bullets.text: Every workplace operates within a framework of regulatory standards, clinical guidelines, and organisational procedures. A policy sets out the local process — but professional judgement remains essential.

bullets.label: Familiarise yourself with your organisation's specific protocols
Understand the difference between the policy and the underlying principle
Apply professional judgement when circumstances differ from routine practice

cards.title: Consistency and Reliability in Safe Practice
cards.body: A safe system depends on reliable, repeatable behaviour — regardless of how busy the ward is or how experienced the nurse.

bullets.label: Hand Hygiene
Every time, every patient, every setting. Non-negotiable.
Patient Identification
Verify identity before every procedure, medication, or intervention.
Allergy Checks
Confirm allergies at every encounter — never assume prior verification is sufficient.
Aseptic Technique
Maintain sterile practice consistently, not selectively under pressure.
International employers assess whether safety
bullets.text: International employers assess whether safety behaviours are maintained across shifts and settings — not just when being observed.

cards.title: Translating Evidence into Practice
cards.body: Clinical guidance evolves as new research emerges. Nurses must stay current and avoid relying on outdated habits.

bullets.label: Use current organisational resources and clinical guidelines
Seek clarification when guidance is unclear or conflicting
Participate actively in education and training updates
Recognise that "this is how we've always done it" can place patients at risk

cards.title: Safe Adaptation in a New System
cards.body: An IQN may encounter unfamiliar devices, electronic record systems, medication platforms, or isolation procedures. Safe adaptation is a professional skill — not a weakness.

bullets.label: Request Orientation
Ask for a formal introduction to unfamiliar equipment, systems, and local workflows before independent practice.
Use Supervision Appropriately
Work under supervision until competence is confirmed through practice and assessment.
Confirm Competence First
Never proceed independently with an unfamiliar
bullets.text: Never proceed independently with an unfamiliar task until you have practised and been assessed within the organisation's approved process.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Latha's First Week
cards.body: On her first week in an overseas hospital, Latha is asked to access an implanted port using equipment she has not previously used. Although she understands the general principles, she requests the local procedure and supervised practice before proceeding.

bullets.label: This decision protects the patient while
bullets.text: This decision protects the patient while allowing Latha to develop competence within the organisation's approved process. It reflects professional integrity — not a lack of skill.

bullets.label: What Latha Did Right
Recognised the limits of her current familiarity
Asked for the local procedure document
Requested supervised practice before acting independently
Protected patient safety without refusing the task

cards.title: The Four Pillars of Safe International Practice
cards.body: Know Your Standards

bullets.label: Understand the regulatory and organisational policies that govern your workplace.
Behave Consistently
Apply core safety behaviours every time — across every shift, every patient, every setting.
Use Current Evidence
Follow current guidelines and resources — not habit or outdated practice.
Seek Orientation
Ask for supervision and confirm competence before practising independently in unfamiliar areas.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: 📋 Policies + Judgement

bullets.label: Policies guide practice; professional judgement adapts it to individual patient situations.
🔄 Consistent Safety
Core safety behaviours must never be compromised by workload, experience, or familiarity.
📚 Evidence-Led
Update your practice as clinical evidence evolves — never rely on habit alone.
🤝 Ask for Help
Seeking orientation and supervision in a new system is a hallmark of professional competence.
Section 1 Complete — Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) Programme 2

cards.title: Clinical Risk Assessment and Early Escalation
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 2 · Level 2

bullets.label: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments — International Qualified Nurse (IQN)
SECTION 2 · STUDENT LEARNING NOTES

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Use Structured Assessments
Apply risk assessment tools appropriately across clinical settings.
Recognise Deterioration
Identify early indicators of patient decline or infection.
Prioritise Safety Actions
Take immediate and appropriate action when risk is identified.
Escalate Clearly
Use structured communication to escalate concerns effectively.

cards.title: Dynamic Risk Assessment
cards.body: Risk is not static — it changes as patient condition, treatment, and environment evolve. A patient safely mobilising in the morning may become dizzy after medication or develop new weakness by afternoon.

bullets.label: Key principle: Repeat your assessment whenever
bullets.text: Key principle: Repeat your assessment whenever the condition, treatment, or environment changes — not just at scheduled intervals.

cards.title: Recognising Early Deterioration
cards.body: Early Warning Signs to Watch For

bullets.label: Altered or rising respiratory rate
New-onset confusion or agitation
Reduced urine output
Fever or signs of infection
Low oxygen saturation (SpO₂)
Increasing or uncontrolled pain
A general sense the patient is becoming unwell
Always compare findings against the patient's baseline and act on concerning trends — not isolated values.

cards.title: Escalation Using ISBAR
cards.body: ISBAR provides a structured framework for communicating patient concerns clearly and efficiently to medical teams.

bullets.label: I — Identify
State who you are and identify the patient clearly.
S — Situation
Describe the current concern or change in condition.
B — Background
Provide relevant clinical history and context.
A — Assessment
Share your clinical assessment of what is happening.
R — Recommendation
State clearly what action or assistance you require.
If the response does not match the urgency of the concern, continue to escalate through the appropriate chain.

cards.title: Listening to Patients and Families
cards.body: Why Their Perspective Matters

bullets.label: Patients and families often notice subtle
bullets.text: Patients and families often notice subtle changes before clinical measurements become abnormal. They know the patient's normal behaviour, mood, and function better than any chart.

bullets.label: Concerns raised by family should always be heard and assessed
Dismissing them can delay recognition of deterioration
It erodes trust and undermines person-centred care

cards.title: Clinical Example: Mr Evans
cards.body: "He is not himself." — Mr Evans's daughter

bullets.label: Mr Evans presents with normal blood pressure
bullets.text: Mr Evans presents with normal blood pressure but is newly confused and breathing faster than earlier. His daughter's concern raises a flag.

bullets.label: Repeat Observations
Re-assess vital signs and document the trend, not just the current reading.
Assess for Infection
Consider sepsis screening — confusion and raised respiratory rate are early indicators.
Escalate Using ISBAR
Request urgent medical review using structured communication.

cards.title: Assessment vs. Escalation
cards.body: The Complete Clinical Picture

bullets.label: Effective nursing decisions rely on combining
bullets.text: Effective nursing decisions rely on combining structured tools with clinical judgement. A score alone cannot replace the nurse's direct observation and interpretation of context.

bullets.label: Tools support decision-making — they do not replace it
Trends are more informative than single readings
Act on the full clinical picture

cards.title: NCLEX Connection: What to Remember
cards.body: These concepts are directly tested in NCLEX and international nursing competency assessments.

bullets.label: 🔁 Continuous Assessment
Risk assessment is an ongoing process, not a one-time event. Reassess with every change.
📈 Trends Over Single Values
Deterioration patterns matter more than a single abnormal reading. Monitor and document trends.
📢 Structured Escalation
Use ISBAR every time. Clear, structured communication improves patient safety outcomes.
👂 Patient Voice
Always listen to patients and families. Their insight can be the earliest clinical warning sign.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Risk assessment is continuous

bullets.label: Reassess whenever the patient's condition, environment, or treatment changes.
Trends and subtle changes matter
Do not wait for a severely abnormal value — act on the emerging pattern.
Escalate using structured communication
ISBAR ensures your concern is heard clearly and acted upon promptly.
Listen to patients and families
Their observations are a valid and important part of the clinical picture.
GNPS Program 2 · Section 2 Complete — Proceed to Section 3: Safe Medication Administration

cards.title: Safe Communication, Documentation & Incident Management
cards.body: Section 3 · Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 2 · Level 2 – Internationally Qualified Nurse

bullets.label: CREATING SAFE HEALTHCARE ENVIRONMENTS

cards.title: Why Communication Matters
cards.body: Communication failures are a leading cause of preventable patient harm. For internationally qualified nurses, mastering accurate handover, objective documentation, and clear information exchange is essential to patient safety.

bullets.label: Good communication makes the patient's current risks visible to everyone involved in care.
Clinical Handover
Deliver concise, accurate, and structured clinical handover
Documentation
Record safety information objectively and promptly
Closed-Loop Comms
Use read-back techniques for critical information
Incident Reporting
Participate constructively in reporting and review processes

cards.title: Clinical Handover: What to Include
cards.body: Handover should be structured, prioritised, and meaningful — not simply a recitation of facts.

bullets.label: Identify
Patient identity & current condition
Context
Relevant history & recent changes
Risks
Active risks & required monitoring
Actions
Outstanding tasks & confirmed responsibility
The receiving clinician must always have an
bullets.text: The receiving clinician must always have an opportunity to ask questions and confirm responsibility before handover is complete.

cards.title: Documentation Standards
cards.body: Every record must be:

bullets.label: Timely
Documented promptly after the event
Accurate & Factual
Reflect what was assessed, the action taken, and patient response
Attributable
Clearly linked to the author who provided care
Objective
Replace labels like "non-compliant" with factual descriptions

cards.title: Closed-Loop Communication
cards.body: A structured technique to eliminate misunderstanding during high-stakes exchanges — especially in emergencies, telephone orders, or noisy clinical environments.

bullets.label: Sender Gives Instruction
Receiver Reads Back
Sender Confirms Accuracy
Cycle Continues
This simple loop reduces errors significantly
bullets.text: This simple loop reduces errors significantly when managing urgent instructions, particularly for high-risk medications or time-critical decisions.

cards.title: Incident & Near-Miss Reporting
cards.body: The Reporting Principle

bullets.label: An incident report complements — but never replaces — clinical documentation. Patient care always comes first.
The report then records relevant facts so that
bullets.text: The report then records relevant facts so that patterns and contributing factors can be systematically reviewed and addressed.

bullets.label: Near misses are valuable learning opportunities — they expose system weaknesses before harm can occur.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Telephone Order for High-Risk Medicine

bullets.label: Recognise the Risk
The line is unclear and the dose sounds unusual — the nurse does not guess.
Apply Closed-Loop
The nurse reads back: patient details, medicine name, dose, route, and timing.
Prescriber Corrects
One digit is corrected — a potentially harmful error is prevented.
Document & Report
The order is documented per policy, and the communication risk is reported to the shift leader.

cards.title: Common Documentation Pitfalls
cards.body: Replace Subjective Labels With Facts

bullets.label: Objective language protects patients, colleagues, and the nurse's professional accountability.
❌ "Difficult patient"
Replace with: "Patient refused medication and stated concerns about side effects."
❌ "Non-compliant"
Replace with: "Patient did not attend dressing change at 10:00. Reason documented."

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Structured Handover

bullets.label: Supports continuity of care and reduces risk at transition points
Objective Documentation
Record facts, actions taken, and patient responses — always
Read-Back Technique
Repeat critical information to confirm accuracy in every high-stakes exchange
Report Near Misses
Every near miss is a chance to strengthen the system before harm occurs
NCLEX Tip: Communication, documentation, and
bullets.text: NCLEX Tip: Communication, documentation, and incident management questions frequently appear in the Safe and Effective Care Environment domain.

decks.title: Delivering Culturally Safe and Patient-Centred Safety Care
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 2 - Level 2 - Section 4 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Delivering Culturally Safe & Patient-Centred Care
cards.body: Section 4 — GNPS Programme 2, Level 2 | Equipping international nurses to communicate safely, bridge cultural gaps, and keep every patient at the centre of care.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify Barriers
Recognise communication barriers — language, literacy, disability, culture — that affect patient safety.
Use Interpreters
Apply professional interpretation and accessible information appropriately in clinical settings.
Involve Patients
Engage patients in infection prevention, risk reduction, and shared decision-making.
Balance Respect & Safety
Honour cultural preferences whilst upholding evidence-based, non-negotiable safety standards.

cards.title: Communication Access
cards.body: Language barriers are a significant patient safety risk. Knowing when and how to use the right communication support is a core clinical skill.

bullets.label: ✅ Professional Interpreters
Required for complex or high-risk conversations
Maintain accuracy and confidentiality
Available in person, by phone, or video
⚠️ Family Members as Translators
May provide emotional support — but not clinical translation
Risk of inaccuracy, omission, or confidentiality breach
Never rely on family for high-risk information exchange
Also adapt materials for hearing, vision, cognitive, and literacy needs.

cards.title: Shared Safety — Patients as Partners
cards.body: Safety is a shared responsibility. Nurses should actively invite patient participation — not assume it will happen automatically.

bullets.label: Confirm Identity
Ask patients to state their name and date of birth at every key interaction.
Hand Hygiene Check
Patients can — and should — feel empowered to ask: "Have you cleaned your hands?"
Report Allergies & Changes
Encourage patients to speak up about allergies and any new or worsening symptoms.
Post-Discharge Care
Ensure patients understand wound or device care before leaving — with demonstration and return demonstration.

cards.title: CULTURAL SAFETY
cards.body: Ask, Don't Assume

bullets.label: Culturally safe care begins with self-awareness
bullets.text: Culturally safe care begins with self-awareness and respectful enquiry. A patient's background does not predict their beliefs or preferences.

bullets.label: Ask: "What matters most to you about your care?" — rather than assuming based on ethnicity or religion.
Accommodate cultural preferences wherever clinically possible
Clearly explain any non-negotiable safety requirements
Document preferences and communicate them to the wider team

cards.title: The Teach-Back Method
cards.body: Teach-back is one of the most effective tools for confirming patient understanding — particularly for medication, infection prevention, and discharge instructions.

bullets.label: Nurse Explains
Clear, jargon-free instruction
Nurse Confirms
Corrects gaps and re-explains
Patient Demonstrates
Explains or shows in own words
Key principle: Teach-back is not a test of the
bullets.text: Key principle: Teach-back is not a test of the patient — it tests whether the nurse's explanation was effective. If the patient cannot recall correctly, the nurse re-teaches.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Discharge with a Wound Drain
cards.body: Putting it all together — a patient with limited English is discharged with a wound drain.

bullets.label: Arrange an Interpreter
A professional interpreter is booked — not a family member — to ensure accuracy throughout discharge education.
Demonstrate & Provide Visual Aids
The nurse demonstrates hand hygiene and drain care, then provides picture-based written instructions for home reference.
Apply Teach-Back
The patient is asked to show and explain each
bullets.text: The patient is asked to show and explain each step. A misunderstanding about when to seek help is identified and corrected before discharge.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: 🗣 Communication Support

bullets.label: Always provide professional interpreters or adapted materials for high-risk clinical information.
🤝 Invite Participation
Respectfully engage every patient in their own safety — identity checks, hygiene, reporting changes.
🌏 Ask, Don't Assume
Cultural safety means enquiring — not inferring — what matters to each individual patient.
✅ Use Teach-Back
Confirm understanding by asking patients to demonstrate or explain in their own words before discharge.

cards.title: End-of-Programme Summary
cards.body: GNPS Programme 2 — Level 2 Complete

bullets.label: You have successfully strengthened four core competencies across this programme:
Risk Assessment
Identifying and responding to clinical and environmental risks before harm occurs.
Infection Prevention
Applying international standards — hand hygiene, PPE, aseptic technique, isolation protocols.
Safety Communication
Delivering clear, culturally safe information to patients, families, and multidisciplinary teams.
Incident Management
Participating in reporting, reflection, and systemic learning when things go wrong.

cards.title: Ready for Level 3
cards.body: From Safe Practice to Leading Safer Systems

bullets.label: Level 3 moves beyond individual safe practice.
bullets.text: Level 3 moves beyond individual safe practice. You will develop skills to lead quality improvement, contribute to global safety initiatives, and support colleagues in building safer healthcare environments.

bullets.label: Completing Level 2 means you are equipped to
bullets.text: Completing Level 2 means you are equipped to practise safely, communicate effectively, and advocate for every patient — wherever in the world you work.
